Two things. Insulate the walls. Staple that stuff up and you can even vapour barrier it if you are concerned about dust from the insulation.

The other thing is the roof. Are the rafters exposed and can you see the roof? If so, it would be a good idea to put a ceiling in and insulate above it. Also, you'll want to look at making sure the area above your new ceiling has proper ventilation. Are there roof vents? Soffit vents? You kind of want this kind of air flow.

Edit: I'm not sure about codes. It is best to check with city hall to see what is required in your area. You can basically ask them the same questions you asked here.

There are no soffit vents (1950s cape if that helps) but there is a ridge vent. The rafters are exposed. Do you think I should put a ceiling in where the joists are (horizontal beams in your linked picture) and put down insulation there, leaving vents for air to circulate up?

Heat rises, so it will go out of the ridge vent naturally, but without soffit vents, you're not pulling air back in, so you aren't getting the full benefit from the ridge vent.

"Basically, for every square inch of ridge (exhaust) vent you must balance it with at least one square inch or more of soffit (intake) vent." http://www.cor-a-vent.com/pdf/balancedventilation.pdf

As always, Google knows all.

Should you put a ceiling up? Yes. From seeing your other reply about temperatures, that will help a lot.

The space above the ceiling will need good air circulation. Without it, it can get humid up there - and we don't want that. Ideally, roof/attic areas are provided air flow through natural convection. Heat rises and escapes through a roof vent. This causes a vacuum and air is pulled in through the soffit vents. Some people will put a spinner of the roof. This helps pull air out of the space, but you need a place air can get in.

I mentioned my old studio in another reply here. I finished basic construction in the winter. At the time I didn't consider roof area air circulation. It totally slipped my mind because I was focusing on acoustics and other things for the studio aspect of the build. The first few days of summer I had water pooling on the vapour barrier on an unfinished section of the ceiling. This was a basic A frame roof and I was planning on re-roofing the building. As a stop gap, I put a large vent on one end of the building and another on the other side with an electric fan pushing air out of the space. The fan was on a timer and only went on during the day. This fixed the problem until roof vents could be installed. It also helped keep the studio space cool because it was no longer wearing a 45+ degree hat.

ISPs work by tapping into an international network of a few data points. I don't have a map on hand, but there are between 5 and 7 of these meshed points all around the US, and there are also some overseas, but we'll talk about those later. These data points are connected by high-speed backbone lines, which are made with fiber cabling so that they can transfer mass data at high speeds. Additionally, each point has a connection to more than 1 other point, so that if one point goes down as little of the overall network goes down as possible.

Your ISP will choose a specific method of communication to get the data to you. At this point, our common methods are Fiber delivery, Cable delivery, and Satellite delivery.

Let's look at all 3:

Fiber delivery is exceptionally fast, but costs more to install than other methods of reception. With fiber delivery, optical fiber is placed all the way to your home, allowing for up to 1Gb/s connection speeds (if your equipment supports that high of speeds)

Cable delivery is pretty fast, and uses existing cabling to actually deliver the data. Typically, you'll be getting your internet from the same place you'll be getting your cable from (Time Warner, Comcast). You'll need a piece of equipment called a Cable Modem, which will allow your ethernet hardware such as your computers and routers to interface with the coaxial cable. Speeds I think max around 300Mb/s, but I'm really not sure. This is probably the most common method of internet delivery right now.

Satellite internet works based on, you guessed it, satellites. Similar to satellite TV, internet traffic goes through satellites orbiting the earth and are beamed down to your local dish. The only bad thing about these connections is that the latency (how long it takes your data to reach others and how long it takes others' data to reach you) is very high, in the realm of Seconds (my latency on a cable connection is around 50 milliseconds).

Now, as far as establishing your own company. AFAIK, it would be cost prohibitive. ISPs provide your link into the backbones that run across the world, and just owning a cable modem won't give you access to the internet. When you send out network traffic from your home connection, that traffic first goes to the ISP, which then sends your request through the internet backbones. The same path is followed in reverse for returning data. An ISP is required for network access, as they're the ones who have made the large purchase and are renting out their services, if that makes sense.

Mainly there are 14 companies that 'are' the Internet. These are called Tier 1 Networks.

These companies own and maintain large networks of fiber optic cables and data centers. They get their name and distinction of being a Tier 1 provider by entering into agreements to not charge other Tier 1 providers money to access their network, in exchange for free access to their network. This means that a tier 1 network is a network that can reach every other network on the Internet without purchasing IP transit or paying anyone.

If you wanted access to these networks you can call up one of the providers and get a quote to purchase a specific sum of bandwidth. (i.e. 10Gbps)
